paper_title: Memory as Weights: Internalizing Long-Term History for Streaming Videos

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Streaming vision-language models (VLMs) must continuously integrate information from the past while remaining responsive to current observations and user queries. Existing memory mechanisms typically compress, retrieve, or cache historical observations and reintroduce them into the input context, forcing historical memory and current observations to compete for limited context. We propose MaLoW, a streaming memory framework that instead internalizes historical context into evolving lightweight parameter updates. MaLoW uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to incrementally consolidate incoming video observations into fixed-size LoRA weights, allowing historical information to be carried forward without revisiting the full video stream. In doing so, MaLoW represents history as weights, while keeping the current observation as input. To support training, we further construct MaLoW-Instruct, a large-scale streaming video dataset containing 381K question-answer pairs over 56K videos. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate that MaLoW achieves strong performance on OVO-Bench, StreamingBench, and StreamArena. On the backward split of OVO-Bench, MaLoW outperforms prior memory approaches by 3.9% to 11.8% across different video backbones while incurring only modest latency overhead. Beyond streaming video understanding, MaLoW also generalizes to vision-language-action models, improving the action success rate on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: By continuously processing an input video stream and responding to user queries, streaming vision-language model (VLM) must reason over what has already happened, interpret what is happening now, and remain attentive to what may happen next. Such capabilities are central to key tasks ranging from streaming video understanding (Niu et al., 2025) to interactive AI assistants (Lab, 2026) and robotic planning (Li et al., 2025), where responses and decisions must be made online under latency and memory constraints. Streaming VLMs have thus emerged as an important research frontier. Recent work has shown that offline VLMs can be adapted to describe ongoing activities in streaming videos (Shen et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026), while instruction fine-tuning can further enable models to monitor future events (Li et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). Despite these efforts, fundamental open problem remains: how should streaming VLM remember? As in the offline setting, an effective memory mechanism must preserve important visual information within bounded memory footprint. The streaming setting, however, introduces additional challenges. First, memory must evolve incrementally as new observations arrive, rather than being repeatedly recomputed from the full history. Second, historical information must be incorporated without crowding out the current observation (see Fig. 1-2). Finally, practical memory mechanism should introduce minimal inference overhead. To address these challenges, we propose MaLoW (Memory as LoRA Weights), framework that internalizes historical context into evolving lightweight parameter updates of streaming VLM, as illustrated in Fig. 1-1. MaLoW incrementally consolidates incoming observations into fixed-size LoRA weights, allowing accumulated history to be carried forward without revisiting the full video stream. The base VLM architecture and parameters stay unchanged and only the lightweight LoRA memory evolves over time. More fundamentally, rather than placing memory and current observations in competition within the same context window, as in prior work (Guan et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a), MaLoW represents history as weights 1 Figure 1 (1): MaLoW internalizes the history context into time-evolving, lightweight parameter updates (LoRA) of streaming VLM. At each step, the streaming VLM takes the current observation and user query as input, and performs inference using the updated LoRA weights. (2): By separating memory from the input, MaLoW preserves the performance on real-time perception while significantly improves the performance of memory-critical, backward tracing tasks. while keeping the current observation as input. At each step, the model takes the current observation and user query as input and performs inference using the updated LoRA weights that encode historical information. By separating historical memory from the input context, MaLoW preserves the models capacity to attend to current observations while retaining information from the past (Fig. 1-2), with only modest inference overhead. Specifically, MaLoW employs recurrent HyperNetwork (Ha et al., 2017) to efficiently generate the LoRA weights that encode historical information. At each time step, the incoming video clip and its textual context are first compressed into compact representation, which is then used to update set of recurrent hidden states. To model the temporal dynamics of these hidden states, MaLoW maintains two parallel branches: state-space model (Yang et al., 2024) for modeling local temporal dependencies, and gated summation branch for preserving global historical semantics. The resulting states are mapped through linear projection to the LoRA weights used by the VLM. To facilitate training, we further construct MaLoW-Instruct, comprehensive streaming video dataset containing 381K question-answer (QA) pairs over 56K videos, by adapting public offline video understanding datasets to the streaming setting. To evaluate our framework, we conduct extensive experiments across benchmarks and settings. MaLoW demonstrates state-of-the-art results on streaming video benchmarks, including OVO-Bench (Niu et al., 2025), StreamingBench (Lin et al., 2026) and StreamArena (Zhang et al., 2026d). On the backward split of OVO-Bench, for example, MaLoW outperforms prior memory approaches by 3.9%11.8% across different video backbones, while incurring modest latency overhead. Across base VLMs ranging from 0.8B to 11B parameters, MaLoW yields consistent performance gains. Beyond streaming video understanding, we further extend MaLoW to the Vision-Language-Action (VLA) setting, where incorporating historical observations and action trajectories improves the action success rate on Simpler (Li et al., 2025) WidowX by 9.3%. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose MaLoW, new streaming memory framework that internalizes historical context into evolving LoRA weights, introducing distinct design in which history is represented as weights while current observations remain as input. We develop recurrent HyperNetwork that incrementally updates LoRA memory from streaming video and other context. We also construct MaLoW-Instruct, large-scale training dataset for streaming video understanding, which we will release publicly. We demonstrate that MaLoW achieves competitive results across streaming video benchmarks, attains consistent gains over diverse base VLMs, and generalizes to VLA settings.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Vision-Language Models. Vision-language models (VLMs) (Liu et al., 2023; Alayrac et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2025b; Clark et al., 2026; Qwen Team, 2026) unify diverse visual understanding and reasoning tasks through natural-language interface. Among these tasks, long-video understanding (Zhou et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2 2025) is particularly challenging because models must preserve and reason over information spanning extended temporal contexts. Prior works (Qian et al., 2024; He et al., 2024; Song et al., 2024) have explored various memory and contextmanagement mechanisms for this offline long video understanding setting. Our work builds on pretrained VLMs and equips them with an evolving long-term memory that is needed in the streaming video setting and incrementally updated as new observations arrive. Streaming VLMs with Memory. Recent works on streaming VLMs (Xia et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026) explore several complementary directions, including constructing higher-quality instruction-tuning data, designing architectures tailored to streaming inputs, and incorporating stronger video encoders. More recent studies (Lu et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026) show that strong VLMs with small local video window yield surprisingly strong performance on real-time questions on existing streaming video benchmarks. Another line of work focuses on the memory mechanisms. Some methods compress historical visual observations into textual summaries or memories (Liu et al., 2026; Guan et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026), while others reduce the accumulated visual tokens through clustering or token merging (Zhang et al., 2024). Additional approaches organize historical information into hierarchical memory structures (Zeng et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Xie et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2026), or maintain fixed-size memory buffer that selectively preserves useful historical observations (Qian et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025). Despite their differences, these methods generally address the growing streaming context by compressing historical information into bounded token budget. In contrast, we represent long-term memory directly in model weights. Concurrent work (Chen et al., 2026) similarly moves long-term memory outside the attention context. However, it stores historical information in separate test-time-training (TTT) branch with online-updated fast weights. In contrast, our method directly internalizes history into the VLM itself by dynamically generating low-rank parameter adaptations, without introducing separate memory branch. Low-Rank Adaptation and Context Internalization. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2022) has been widely adopted as parameter-efficient approach for adapting pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) to downstream tasks or new domains (Dettmers et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2025). Recently, several works have explored using LoRA as representation for encoding data-specific patterns (Shrestha et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2026) or contextual information (Charakorn et al., 2026, 2025). These approaches demonstrate that model parameters can be good representation for storing information beyond conventional token-based context. However, they typically require additional optimization when adapting to new pattern, making it difficult to apply them directly to evolving inputs. δ-mem (Lei et al., 2026) explores dynamically representing textual information through LoRA updates without test-time training. Nevertheless, it still relies on access to the historical context during inference. Different from these prior approaches, our work specifically handles the streaming setting, and introduces context internalization mechanism that progressively incorporates incoming visual context into low-rank model representations.

sections.title: 3.2 Our Design: MaLoW
sections.content: We now describe the design of MaLoW, focusing on the single-step update . Conceptually, consists of three parts: (1) the encoding of context Ct1; (2) the update of the hidden state ht; and (3) the decoding of the LoRA weights θt. This is illustrated in Fig. 2-(2-5). Context Encoding. Videos contain substantial redundancy (Shang et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2025). Given the observation Ct1 consisting of video clip and its textual context (e.g., timestamps in text format), we first compress it into compact representation. This is done by first encoding the video and text into their embeddings Vt1 (video) and Tt1 (text) using the vision encoder and the text tokenizer of the VLM. We then learn set of queries to compress Vt1 and Tt1 qt1 = g([Vt1; Tt1; Q]) (4) where qt1 is the resulting compact representation of Ct1. is realized using few self-attention layers, with the concatenated [Vt1, Tt1, Q] as the input (see Fig. 2-2). Hidden-State Update. In interactive settings, new observations arrive continuously over time. An effective memory mechanism should therefore capture both the temporal dependencies among observations and the global semantics accumulated throughout the interaction. To this end, we decompose the hidden state ht into two components: ht = [mt; st], where mt models local temporal dynamics in the stream, while st captures longer-term semantic information. 4 Specifically, mt is modeled by State-Space Model (SSM) using DeltaNet from (Yang et al., 2024). Given qt1 and the previous state mt1, the SSM is updated as mt, ot = SSM(qt1, mt1), (5) where mt denotes the updated state and ot the corresponding output. Through recurrent updates, mt captures the temporal dependencies across the observed stream (see Fig. 2-3). In parallel, st is simply gated summation of qt1, acting as skip connection to allow longer-term memory (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). This is given by st = st1 + βt1qt1 with βt1 = I(cid:2)sim( Vt1, Vt2) β(cid:3) , (6) where βt is binary gate, is the indicator function, and sim( Vt1, Vt2) is the cosine similarity on the averaged pooled Vt1, Vt2. This is shown in Fig. 2-5. LoRA Decoding. Finally, we convert the accumulated historical information, represented by ot and st, into LoRA weights θt using readout function θt = h(ot, st) (7) is realized as linear mapping on top of ot and st normalized with RMSNorm (Zhang & Sennrich, 2019), with an additional learnable gating parameter α applied to the normalized version of st (see Fig. 2-4). The resulting LoRA weights θt will be applied to the VLM at the next time step.

sections.title: 3.4 Training data construction: MaLoW-Instruct
sections.content: To train MaLoW to enable adapted VLMs to retrospect over past observations, preserve relevant information for understanding the present, and support future responses or actions, we construct comprehensive training dataset for streaming video understanding, named as MaLoW-Instruct. Data Sources and Dataset Construction. Our data construction pipeline consists of three main components: (1) question generator, (2) an answer generator, and (3) an verifier (Fig. 3-1). We build on existing video 5 Figure 3 Overview of the MaLoW data pipeline and statistics of MaLoW-Instruct. (1): Our data pipeline consists of Question Generator, an Answer Generator, and Verifier. (2): The distribution of the streaming question timing, the question type, and video source in MaLoW-Instruct. temporal grounding and procedural action datasets that provide event/action timestamps and corresponding descriptions. For each annotated event, the question generator takes the video together with the event description and generates candidate questions about either the target event itself or its surrounding context, an expected answer, along with the question timestamps t. We consider diverse question formats, including open-ended, multiple-choice, and yes/no questions. To prevent data leakage, we filter out the samples used in OVO-Bench (Niu et al., 2025). Given generated question, the answer generator then processes the video up to timestamp and produces model answer. Finally, the verifier takes the generated question, expected answer, model answer, and the video context surrounding the target event to assess both the validity of the question and the correctness of the answer. An unreasonable question or an inconsistent answer typically results in disagreement between the expected answer, generated answer, and supporting video context. We therefore retain only QA pairs that pass the verification stage to form the final training dataset. We use Qwen3.5-122B-A10B (Qwen Team, 2026) as both the question and answer generator, and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B as the verifier. Please see more details in the Appendix B.1 and B.2. Dataset Statistics. MaLoW-Instruct contains 381K instruction samples on 56K videos. We summarize the distributions and statistics of the videos and questions in Fig. 3-2. Approximately 36% of the QA pairs have query timestamps that occur after the corresponding event has ended, providing explicit supervision for learning the MaLoW module to retain and retrieve historical information. Moreover, for many real-time questions, part of the relevant event falls outside the current observation window, further encouraging the model to leverage historical context through MaLoW. The question types are approximately evenly distributed among multiple-choice, open-ended, and yes/no questions. The videos are collected from 14 datasets, among which CosMo-Cap (Wang et al., 2024a), YouCook2 (Zhou et al., 2018), Charades-STA (Gao et al., 2017), and ActivityNet-Captions (Krishna et al., 2017) together account for 62.5% of all videos. More dataset statistics are presented in the Appendix B.3.

sections.title: 4.1 Streaming Video Understanding
sections.content: Benchmarks. Following the prior works (Shen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a), we evaluate MaLoW on the Real-Time split of StreamingBench (Lin et al., 2026), as well as the Real-Time and Backward splits of OVO-Bench (Niu et al., 2025). The Backward splits of OVO-Bench mostly focus on retrospect to the past and comprise three tasks: Episodic Memory (EPM), Action Sequence Identification (ASI), and Hallucination Detection (HLD). Among them, EPM is particularly well suited for assessing the effectiveness of the memory mechanism introduced by MaLoW. Experiment Protocol. We build MaLoW on top of diverse set of VLMs, including models pre-trained for offline video understanding (Qwen3-VL-4B (Bai et al., 2025) and Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026)) and models designed for streaming video (VideoChat3-4B (Li et al., 2026) and MOSS-VL-Realtime-11B (Wang et al., 2026)). We apply rank-8 LoRA to the MLP in each attention layer and v_proj layers in each self-attention layer. For Qwen3.5-9B, we additionally apply LoRA to the in_proj_qkv_proj layers in its linear-attention blocks. For MOSS-VL, we additional apply v_proj layers in each cross-attention layer. We use four-layer self-attention network as the aggregator, with hidden dimension of 512 and eight attention heads. For each layer of the base model, we learn an independent query and maintain corresponding hidden state. We instantiate the SSM using four-layer DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2024) with hidden dimension of 512. To generate the LoRA parameters, we learn separate linear projection layers for each target module and LoRA rank component. We train MaLoW on the training data introduced in Sec. 3.4 for 2,800 steps with total batch size of 64. We use the Adam optimizer with peak learning rate of 8 105 and cosine learning-rate schedule. The videos are sampled at 1 fps during training and inference of MaLoW. Each Ct is 2-second video clip. Additional implementation details are provided in the Appendix C.1. Baselines. We categorize the baselines into four groups according to the model types and how they manage historical visual context during streaming inference. 1. Offline VLMs. This category includes LLaVA-Video-7B (Zhang et al., 2025b), LongVU-7B (Shen et al., 2025), Qwen3-VL-4B (Bai et al., 2025), and Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026). We compare to these models for their strong video understanding capabilities, acquired through large-scale video-text pretraining. We evaluate their pretrained checkpoints by treating streaming videos as offline inputs. 2. Streaming VLMs with Long-term (Full) Context. This category includes VideoLLM-Online (Chen et al., 2024a), Streamo (Xia et al., 2026), VideoChat3 (Li et al., 2026), and MOSS-VL-Realtime (Wang et al., 7 2026). These methods preserve historical observations directly in the inference context as memory for streaming video understanding, and for short videos often retaining the entire video history. As the stream grows, this leads to an ever expanding context window and substantial memory and computational overhead. We note that VideoChat3 uses local context window on OVO-Bench, while retaining the full historical context on StreamingBench. 3. Streaming VLMs with Local Context Window. This category includes Mage-VL (Yang et al., 2026), SimpleStream (Shen et al., 2026), and AURA (Lu et al., 2026). We compare to these models for their strong real-time performance, achieved by retaining only the most recent observations within fixed local window of approximately 430 seconds. Historical observations that fall outside the local window are evicted (Xu et al., 2026). 4. Streaming VLMs with Local Context Window and Memory Mechanism. This category includes FlashVStream (Zhang et al., 2024), Dispider (Qian et al., 2025), TimeChat-Online (Yao et al., 2025), StreamForest (Zeng et al., 2026), JoyAI-VL (Yao et al., 2026), HERMES (Zhang et al., 2026a), ThinkStream (Liu et al., 2026), VST (Guan et al., 2026), OASIS (Liang et al., 2026) and StreamTTT (Chen et al., 2026). Similar to our design, these methods retain most recent observations in local context window while compressing historical information into more compact memory representation, such as textual summaries or condensed visual features. Among them, the concurrent work StreamTTT is most relevant. StreamTTT stores historical information in an online-updated test-time-training (TTT) branch while retaining the most recent visual tokens as the current observation. MaLoW achieves state-of-the-art results. As shown in Table 1, MaLoW establishes strong performance across streaming video benchmarks. MaLoW (MOSS-VL-Realtime-11B) and MaLoW (Qwen3-VL-4B) achieve new state-of-the-art scores of 74.5% and 84.8% on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench, respectively, while MaLoW (Qwen3.5-9B) attains the highest EPM score of 63.6% among all compared methods. We highlight key comparisons at matched model scales. At the 4B scale, the MaLoW (Qwen3-VL-4B) surpasses the concurrent work StreamTTT-4B (Chen et al., 2026) by 3.9% and 3.5% on the backward split of the OVO-bench and StreamingBench, respectively. At the 7-9B scale, the MaLoW (Qwen3.5-9B) outperforms the previous memory-based method OASIS-8B (Liang et al., 2026) and local window-based method AURA-8B (Lu et al., 2026) by 9.2% and 6.0% on the backward split of the OVO-bench, respectively. At the 11B scale, MaLoW (MOSS-VL-Real-11B) improves over its base MOSS-VL-Real-11B by 2.2% and 1.4% on the Real-Time split and EPM task of OVO-Bench, respectively. We recognize that on the OVO-Bench real-time split, MaLoW (Qwen3-VL-4B) and MaLoW (Qwen3.5-9B) underperform StreamTTT-4B and AURA-8B, respectively. We hypothesize that these baselines may have benefited from fine-tuning their base VLMs, whereas MaLoW keeps the base VLMs intact. Collectively, these results show that MaLoW is particularly effective on memory-critical tasks while retaining competitive performance on real-time perception. Importantly, the gains are consistent across model scales from 4B to 11B and across base VLMs pre-trained for both offline video understanding (Qwen series) and streaming video understanding (VideoChat3 and MOSS-VL-Realtime). MaLoW offers lightweight memory patch. Across different base VLMs, MaLoW introduces only 1.4%-4.0% additional parameters. The pretrained backbone architecture and parameters remain unchanged, while historical information is encoded entirely through the evolving LoRA weights. Preserving the backbone helps retain its pretrained capabilities and minimizes interference with real-time perception. Moreover, widespread LoRA support in modern inference frameworks facilitates efficient deployment. MaLoW incurs minor inference overhead. We profile the streaming inference latency of MaLoW (Qwen3.5-9B) and four baselines on 100 deterministically sampled questions from OVO-Bench. At each query timestamp t, we measure the time required to process the current observation, prefill the KV cache, and decode the first token. For MaLoW, we additionally include the cost of generating and applying the LoRA weights. Further experimental details are provided in Appendix C. In particular, MaLoW outperforms the full-context baseline on real-time perception splits (green cells), demonstrating that MaLoW effectively alleviates the negative effect of history on real-time perception. We further extend MaLoW to robotic planning, where it is used to internalize historical visual observations and action trajectory for action prediction. Following VLM4VLA (Zhang et al., 2026b), we adapt Qwen3.5-2B (Qwen Team, 2026) by attaching lightweight MLP action decoder and fine-tuning the VLM backbone, resulting in our baseline model, Q3.5-2B-MLP. We then train MaLoW on top of Q3.5-2B-MLP using the Bridge subset of OXE. During this stage, the VLM backbone is frozen and receives only the current observation, while MaLoW and the MLP action decoder are optimized to internalize historical observations and action trajectories and produce more accurate action trajectories. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we presented MaLoW, new memory framework for streaming VLMs. Rather than repeatedly injecting compressed or retrieved history into the input context, MaLoW represents history as LoRA weights while keeping the current observation as input. This separation provides natural way to carry long-term information forward without revisiting the full video stream or continually expanding the context window. It also yields lightweight memory patch: the base VLM architecture and parameters remain unchanged, while only the compact LoRA weights evolve over time. To realize this design, we developed recurrent HyperNetwork that incrementally updates LoRA weights, together with MaLoW-Instruct, large-scale streaming video dataset containing 381K QA pairs over 56K videos. MaLoW achieves strong results across streaming video understanding benchmarks, with substantial gains on memory-critical tasks and only modest inference overhead. We further show that the same memory mechanism transfers to VLA models, where incorporating historical context improves action success. We hope that MaLoW offers useful perspective on long-term memory for streaming VLMs: beyond asking what information should be stored or retrieved, we can also reconsider where memory should reside, in this case, directly within evolving model weights.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: This appendix provides the mathematical interpretation, dataset documentation, implementation details, and additional empirical results supporting MaLoW. The materials are organized as follows: Appendix A: Mathematical Interpretation. Historical context as read operator, its realization through low-rank MLP updates, online memory updates, and extensions to normalized attention and backbone computation. Appendix B: Additional Dataset Details. Video sources, the data pipeline and annotation construction, and statistics of MaLoW-Instruct. Appendix C: Additional Experiment Details. Model architecture, training and evaluation settings, the visionlanguage-action setting, different VLM scales and sources, the memory stress test, and streaming inference speed profiling. Appendix D: Additional Experiments. Ablations of LoRA placement and rank, memory architecture, observation windows, and state-update frequency; analyses of latency, hidden-state evolution, and real-time perception; and additional qualitative results.

We primarily build upon these large-scale collections rather than gathering every underlying dataset independently, as they already consolidate videos from diverse academic sources and have undergone prior curation and preprocessing, providing more scalable and reliable starting point for dataset construction. To prevent evaluation contamination, we further filter out videos that overlap with those used in OVO-Bench (Niu et al., 2025). In contrast, StreamingBench and StreamArena do not overlap with any of our video sources and therefore require no additional filtering. After aggregating all sources and removing duplicate and overlapping videos, the resulting dataset contains 55,867 unique videos drawn from 14 underlying video datasets. detailed breakdown of the video distribution is provided in Table 5. B.2 Data Pipeline and Annotation Construction As illustrated in Figure 3-1, our data construction pipeline consists of three components: Question Generator, an Answer Generator, and Verifier. To construct the streaming video training dataset, we begin with an event description associated with specific temporal interval. These descriptions are obtained either from the original annotations of the 14 datasets described in Section B.1, or from the questionanswer pairs provided by TimeLens and ET-Instruct. Question Generation. We first prompt the Question Generator to generate new question for target event, conditioned on the full video, the event description, and its corresponding temporal interval. By observing the full video, the Question Generator can leverage both the target event and its surrounding visual context to construct question that is grounded in the video content. The prompt explicitly controls the question type, which is sampled from four categories: open-ended, multiple-choice, Yes/No, and counting questions. Along with each generated question, the Question Generator also produces an expected answer, which is subsequently used during the verification stage. To cover different temporal reasoning scenarios, we further assign each question randomly sampled question-timestamp type from three categories: past, real-time, and future. Given target event spanning the interval [tstart, tend], past question is assigned timestamp > tend, requiring the model to retrospectively recall an event that has already occurred. real-time question is assigned timestamp [tstart, tend], such that the target event is ongoing when the question is asked. future question is assigned timestamp < tstart, requiring the model either to anticipate future event 21 Table 6 Distribution of questions across timestamp classes. The exact question timestamp is then randomly sampled from the temporal range corresponding to the selected timestamp type. We use Qwen3.5-122B-A10B (Qwen Team, 2026) as the Question Generator. For question generation, we launch four parallel workers, each serving one Qwen3.5-122B-A10B instance with vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) on two H200 GPUs. Answer Generation. After obtaining the generated questions and their corresponding timestamps t, we prompt the Answer Generator to produce model answer using only the video content observable up to time t. This setup ensures that the generated answer respects the streaming setting and does not access visual information occurring after the question timestamp. We use Qwen3.5-122B-A10B (Qwen Team, 2026) as the Answer Generator. For answer generation, we launch four parallel workers, each serving one Qwen3.5-122B-A10B instance with vLLM on two H200 GPUs. Verification. After obtaining the generated question and its corresponding model answer, we prompt the Verifier to assess the quality of the generated questionanswer pair. The Verifier takes as input the generated question, the expected answer, the model answer, and the original event description used during question generation. It evaluates both whether the generated question is valid and well grounded in the target event and whether the model answer is consistent with the available evidence. In particular, substantial mismatch between the expected answer and the model answer may indicate either that the generated question is ambiguous or unreasonable, or that the model answer is incorrect. The original event description provides additional grounding information that allows the Verifier to distinguish between these cases and assess the overall validity of the questionanswer pair. For verification, we launch two parallel workers, each serving one Qwen3.5-397B-A17B instance with vLLM on four H200 GPUs. Filtering and Post-Processing. We discard questionanswer pairs for which the Verifier identifies an inconsistency between the expected answer and the model answer, determines that the model answer is incorrect, or judges the generated question to be invalid, ambiguous, or otherwise unreasonable. After filtering, we group questions associated with the same video and question timestamp into multi-turn conversations, which are subsequently used for training. We also include annotations from the offline video understanding from LLaVA-Video-178K to further strengthen the memory mechanism. B.3 Dataset Statistic MaLoW-Instruct contains 381K instruction samples constructed from 56K videos. Table 6 and Table 7 summarize the distribution of questions by timestamp class and question type. In terms of temporal categories, real-time questions constitute the largest proportion (46.1%), followed by past (36.4%) and future (17.4%) questions. These categories correspond to questions posed while the target event is occurring, after the event has occurred, and before the event occurs, respectively. Regarding question types, multiple-choice questions account for the largest proportion (35.0%), while open-ended (34.7%) and Yes/No (30.0%) questions are comparably represented, with counting questions comprising the remaining 14.0%. Table 8 summarizes the statistics of the questions, answers, and video durations in the dataset. Questions contain an average of 70.4 tokens, encoded by the tokenizer from Qwen3.5-9B, while answers are generally concise, with an average of 3.8 tokens. The question timestamps cover wide temporal range, with an average question video length of 57.2 seconds, while the full videos are longer on average at 89.5 seconds, reaching up to 1,673.4 seconds. sections.title: C Additional Experiment Details
sections.content: C.1 Main Experiments In this section, we provide additional experiment details for the main experiments presented in Table 1. Base Models. In the main experiments, we build MaLoW on top of four different models, VideoChat3-4B (Li et al., 2026), Qwen3-VL-4B (Bai et al., 2025), Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026), and MOSS-VL-Realtime11B (Wang et al., 2026). VideoChat3 is video-centric VLM that is further fine-tuned on streaming video understanding data and adopts full self-attention architecture. Qwen3-VL-4B is general-purpose VLM based on full self-attention architecture. Qwen3.5 is general-purpose VLM based on hybrid attention architecture, where self-attention layer is interleaved with every four linear-attention layers. MOSS-VL is video-centric VLM that adapts cross-attention layers to inject visual information into the text tokens, and cross-attention layer is interleaved with every four self-attention layers. Video Preprocessing. During training and evaluation, we sample the video frames at 1 fps, dividing the video frames into non-overlapping two-frame temporal blocks (each Ct is 2-second video clip). We regard the most recent 2-second block as the current observation, which will be sent into the VLMs, while all the rest of the history frames will be sent into the MaLoW to be converted into LoRA weights. For MaLoW (Qwen3-VL-4B), we observe that using longer current-observation windows consistently improves performance on the real-time and backward splits of OVO-Bench (Niu et al., 2025) and StreamingBench (Lin et al., 2026). We therefore use the most recent 8-second clips as the current observations for MaLoW (Qwen3-VL-4B), while the other MaLoW instantiations in the table use the most recent 2 seconds. We hypothesize that these findings, MaLoW (Qwen3-VL-4B) benefiting from longer current-observation windows and the particularly strong performance on StreamingBench, are largely attributable to differences in the architecture and pretraining recipe of the underlying VLMs. We preprocess the video frames with the preprocessor from the corresponding VLMs, with the maximum per-frame pixel budget set to 262,144 for all three versions of MaLoW. 23 Vision Encoder. We use the vision encoder from the corresponding VLMs as the vision encoder to encode each of the temporal blocks into vision tokens. We also use the MLP layers or adaptor from the VLMs to convert the vision tokens into the text semantic space before we send them into the Aggregator. We denote the vision tokens from the temporal block at as Vt. Aggregator. Visual tokens Vt in the temporal block at are concatenated with the learnable queries and the corresponding text embedding Tt of the timestamp of the temporal block. These tokens are first projected to hidden dimension of 512 and processed by four-layer Transformer encoder aggregator with eight attention heads (64 dimensions per head), feed-forward dimension of 2,048, pre-layer normalization, GELU activations. We learn one 512-dimensional query for each of the VLM decoder layers. The query is shared across target modules, and LoRA ranks in the same VLM decoder layer. State-Space Model. We learn four-layer DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2024) with hidden dimension of 512 as the state-space model. Each DeltaNet layer uses four value heads and two key heads, both with head dimension 128. Cosine-Similarity-Based Gating. We determine the gating threshold by profiling the cosine similarity score between two adjecent block from 1000 subset of video from the training data introduced in section 3.4. Across 64,426 transitions between consecutive temporal blocks, the median raw cosine distance, 1 cos( Vt, Vt1), is 0.0542. We therefore set β = 0.05, approximately the median-change operating point. The first temporal block is always retained, while each subsequent block is retained if cos( Vt, Vt1) β. Blocks exhibiting less visual change than this threshold receive zero weight in the residual-history aggregation, whereas the retained blocks are uniformly averaged. The Converter. For each target-module type and each LoRA rank, separate linear output head maps the 512-dimensional representation orm(ot) + αN orm(st) to vector of dimension din + dout. The vector is split into one row of the LoRA factors At Rrdin and Bt Rrdout . These output heads are shared across decoder layers, while layer specificity is supplied by the layer-specific learned queries. Finally, the LoRA at At, where α is lora_alpha, which we set to 16. particular slot at timestamp is calculated with θt = α BT LoRA Application Location. For VideoChat3-4B, we apply rank-8 generated LoRA for the MLP projections (gate_proj, up_proj, and down_proj) and self_attn.v_proj in every attention layer. For the Qwen3VL-4B, we apply rank-8 generated LoRA for the MLP projections (gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj), and self_attn.v_proj in every attention layer. For Qwen3.5-9B, we apply rank-8 generated LoRA for the MLP projections (gate_proj, up_proj, and down_proj) in every attention layer, self_attn.v_proj in fullattention layers, and linear_attn.in_proj_qkv in linear-attention layers. For MOSS-VL-Realtime-11B, we apply rank-8 generated LoRA for the MLP projections (gate_proj, up_proj, and down_proj), and v_proj in every attention layer. We inject the generated LoRA weights into the target linear layers of the frozen base model through customized forward functions. Training Details. We build our training pipeline on top of the Llama-Factory (Zheng et al., 2024). We train MaLoW on the MaLoW-Instruct dataset introduced in Section 3.4 for 2,800 optimization steps with total batch size of 64. Training uses four H200s, per-device batch size of one, and 16 gradient-accumulation steps. We use AdamW with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, ϵ = 108, an peak learning rate of 8 105, cosine learning-rate schedule, and warm-up ratio of 0.1. Training is performed in bfloat16. We set the LoRA regularization factor γ to 0.01. During training, we use the state-space model in its parallel causal form. For each sample, the compact vision representations qt are arranged in chronological order and processed by the four-layer DeltaNet using the chunk-parallel gated-delta-rule kernel and an attention mask for padded blocks. We then select the output at the last valid temporal block for each history observation. This parallel computation is causally equivalent to processing the blocks recurrently while carrying the convolutional and recurrent DeltaNet states, which is the form that is used for online streaming inference. Evaluation Details. Following the evaluation protocols adopted in prior streaming video understanding works (Shen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a), we evaluate MaLoW on the Real-Time split of StreamingBench (Lin et al., 2026), as well as the Real-Time and Backward splits of OVO-Bench (Niu et al., 2025). For StreamingBench, we evaluate on the Real-Time split, which contains 2,500 multiple-choice questions, and 24 use accuracy as metric. For OVO-Bench, both the Backward and Real-Time splits are evaluated with the metric accuracy. The Backward and Real-Time splits consist of 631 and 837 questions. Following prior work, the performance of each split is computed as the macro-average across the tasks belonging to that split, and we additionally report the macro-average performance across the Backward and Real-Time splits in Table 1. The Backward splits of OVO-Bench mostly focus on retrospect to the past and comprise three tasks: Episodic Memory (EPM), Action Sequence Identification (ASI), and Hallucination Detection (HLD). Among them, EPM is particularly well suited for evaluating the memory mechanism introduced by MaLoW, as it directly measures the models ability to retain and retrieve information from earlier observations. We further note that HLD is relatively less challenging because all ground-truth responses are Unable to answer. As result, models can achieve high accuracy on this task by consistently predicting this response, making HLD less discriminative for assessing the effectiveness of long-term memory mechanisms. The trained MaLoW can operate in fully streaming manner by processing the video history block by block using the cached-forward mode of DeltaNet. (Please see the Evaluation details. in the section C.2) To accelerate evaluation, however, we use the same parallel-forward mode employed during training when evaluating on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench. Specifically, for question associated with video prefix [0, ], we treat the interval [0, 2] as historical context and sample it at 1 fps as input to the hypernetwork. The base VLM then receives the question together with two frames sampled from the current observation window [T 2, ]. For the evaluation on the OVO-bench, we follow the prompt example used in lmms-eval (Zhang et al., 2025a), and for the evaluation on the StreamingBench we follow the prompt example used in the official repository. Baselines Re-Evaluation. Among the baselines in Table 1, we re-evaluate MOSS-VL-Realtime-11B (Wang et al., 2026), VideoChat3-4B (Li et al., 2026), and Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026), as these models are also used as the base VLMs for MaLoW. For the remaining baselines, we report the results from their original papers. For Qwen3.5-9B, we sample video frames at 1 fps with maximum per-frame pixel budget of 262,144 and use greedy decoding for answer generation. For VideoChat3-4B, we use the official evaluation code and follow the hyperparameters reported in the paper. On OVO-Bench, we sample frames at 2 fps and retain the 32 most recent frames, with per-frame pixel budget of 4482 and visual-token budget of 80K. On StreamingBench, we sample frames at 4 fps with at most 4,096 frames, using the same per-frame pixel budget of 4482 and visual-token budget of 80K. For MOSS-VL-Realtime-11B, as neither the paper nor the released repository provides an official evaluation script, we evaluate the model on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench using frames sampled at 1 fps with maximum per-frame pixel budget of 262,144. These settings successfully reproduce the reported OVO-Bench performance of VideoChat3 and MOSSVL-Realtime. However, our re-evaluated StreamingBench results are lower than those reported in the corresponding papers. We therefore include both the re-evaluated and paper-reported results in Table 1, with the paper-reported results shown in gray. C.2 MaLoW in VLA setting In this section, we provide more implementation details for the MaLoW in the VLA setting. The results are presented in Table 2. Base VLA Model and Initialization. Inspired by the previous work (Zhang et al., 2026b), we train simple VLA model on top of Qwen3.5-2B, named as Q3.5-2B-MLP, as the starting point of the MaLoW (Q3.5-2B-MLP). The Q3.5-2B-MLP is given the current observation (an image) and text instruction and predicts chunk of four seven-dimensional actions, corresponding to the current action and the following three actions. We learn special tokens as action hidden representations, and VLMs compress the visual observation and the text instruction into the special tokens. An action decoder, which is two-layer MLP that directly regresses normalized robot actions using mean-squared error based on the special tokens. We use the Qwen3.5 preprocessor to preprocess the input image and the text instruction. 25 Q3.5-2B-MLP was trained on the Bridge and RT-1 mixture of the OXE LeRobot dataset (ONeill et al., 2024) for 50,000 optimization steps, with learning rate is 4 105 on action decoder, and 1 104 on LoRA. The learning rate is linearly warmed up for 5,000 steps and then cosine-decayed. Training uses AdamW with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95, ϵ = 108,and weight decay 108. Training is conducted in bfloat16 on four H200 GPUs with per-device batch size of 16 and two gradient-accumulation steps, yielding global batch size of 128. We apply rank-128 LoRA to all linear layers, including the vision tower and multimodal projector, with scaling factor of 256. Q3.5-2B-MLP achieves 59.4% in the Simpler-Bridge with WidowX robot. Observation Preprocessing. For training sample at control step t, the base VLA Model receives the current observation xt and the language instruction, while the MaLoW receives all preceding observations x0, . . . , xt1. We do not impose maximum history length. Bridge trajectories are recorded at 5 Hz, and timestamps are therefore expressed using control period of 0.2 seconds. The current observation is processed through the same single-image preprocessing path as the Q3.5-2B-MLP, while all the historical observations are decoded directly from the episode video and be sent into the MaLoW. All the frames are resized to 224 224, and passed to the Qwen3.5-2B preprocessor. This matches the preprocessing of the historical frames received from SimplerEnv during interactive evaluation. We divide the observation history into consecutive, non-overlapping two-frame blocks, matching the temporal patch size of the Qwen vision encoder. If the history contains an odd number of frames, its final frame is repeated to complete the last block. For example, the history at step = 3 is represented as [x0, x1] and [x2, x2]. Each block is assigned timestamp interval using the true Bridge control clock. committed block is labeled [2jt, (2j + 2)t], where = 0.2 seconds. Vision Encoder. We use frozen copy of the vision tower and vision adaptor from the Q3.5-2B-MLP as the MaLoWs vision encoder. Action-History Conditioning. In addition to visual history, every historical frame is paired with the action that produced it. Specifically, frame xi is paired with the preceding action ai1. The first frame x0 is paired with learned empty-action embedding representing a1. Historical actions undergo the same normalization transformations as the action targets. Each seven-dimensional action is mapped to the visual-token dimension by two-layer MLP with GELU activation. Thus, the input sequence for two-frame temporal block is [V2j, V2j+1, Tj, E(a2j1), E(a2j)], where Vi denotes the visual tokens for frame i, Tj denotes the frozen token embeddings of the blocks timestamp interval, and E() is the action-history MLP. Aggregator. For every temporal block, the visual, timestamp, and action-history tokens are projected to hidden dimension of 512 and processed by four-layer Transformer encoder. The rest of the aggregators details are the same as the one used in section C.1. State-Space Model and the Converter. The state-space model and the converter share the same details as the one used in section C.1. LoRA Application Locations. Because Qwen3.5 interleaves full self-attention and linear-attention layers, the rank 8 generated LoRA is applied to gate_proj, up_proj, and down_proj in every decoder layer, to self_attn.v_proj in full-attention layers, and to linear_attn.in_proj_qkv in linear-attention layers. Training Details. MaLoW (Q3.5-2B-MLP) is trained on the Bridge portion of the OXE LeRobot dataset. Before training, we merge the Q3.5-2B-MLP LoRA adapter into Qwen3.5-2B and load the stage-1 action-decoder weights. The merged Qwen backbone is then frozen. The trainable components in the MaLoW (Q3.5-2B-MLP) are the MaLoW, including the aggregator, action-history encoder, temporal state-space model, and LoRA output heads, together with the action decoder. The complete objective is where = Laction + 0.1 LLoRA, LLoRA = 1 (cid:88) sS (mean As + mean Bs) 26 , is the set of valid generated LoRA slots, and Laction is MSE Loss between the predicted actions and the ground truth actions. We train for 25,000 optimization steps using four H200 GPUs. The per-device batch size is four and gradients are accumulated for four steps, giving total batch size of 64. We use AdamW with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95, ϵ = 108, and weight decay 108 and learning rate of 1 105 in this experiment. We use cosine schedule with 1,500 warm-up steps and final learning rate of 5 107. Training is performed in bfloat16 with FlashAttention-2 and ordinary distributed data parallelism. Evaluation Details. We evaluate MaLoW (Q3.5-2B-MLP) on the four WidowX Bridge tasks in SimplerEnv: Stack Green Block on Yellow Block, Put Carrot on Plate, Put Spoon on Towel, and Put Eggplant in Yellow Basket. Each task contains 24 evaluation episodes, for total of 96 episodes. Evaluation is conducted in fully interactive streaming setting. At environment step zero, no historical context is available, and the model exactly reproduces the Q3.5-2B-MLP policy. At each subsequent step, completed two-frame blocks and the corresponding actions are permanently incorporated into the cached DeltaNet state mt and updated into the global sematic st. If the history ends with an unpaired frame, we duplicate it to form provisional block and generate the current adapter using temporary copy of the recurrent state. At the next step, we discard this temporary update and incorporate the completed two-frame block into the persistent state. The ht state is reset at each episode boundary. The policy predicts four-action chunks and applies action ensembling over horizon of four steps. Because ensembling may cause the action executed by the environment to differ from the most recent raw model prediction, we feed the normalized executed action back to the policy server. This executed action, rather than the unensembled model prediction, is paired with the corresponding observation when constructing subsequent history blocks. C.3 MaLoW with different VLM scales and sources In this section, we provide additional implementation details for the results presented in Table 4. Base Models. In this sections, we use the Gemma-E4B (Gemma Team, 2026) and Qwen3.5-0.8B, Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026) as the base model. LoRA Application Location. For Gemma-E4B, we apply rank-8 generated LoRA for the MLP projections (gate_proj, up_proj, and down_proj) in every attention layer. For Qwen3.5 series, we apply rank-8 generated LoRA for the MLP projections (gate_proj, up_proj, and down_proj) in every attention layer, self_attn.v_proj in full-attention layers, and linear_attn.in_proj_qkv in linear-attention layers. Data, Structural, and Training Details. For the Video Preprocessing, Vision Encoder, Aggregator, State-Space Model, Cosine-similarity-based gating, the Converter, and Training details are share the same details in section C.1. Evaluation Details. For the evaluation on the OVO-bench, we follow the example used in lmms-eval (Zhang et al., 2025a), and for the evaluation on the StreamingBench we follow the example used in the official repository. For question associated with video prefix [0, ], the interval [0, 2] is treated as historical context and sampled at 1 fps for the MaLoW. The base VLM receives the question together with two frames sampled from the current observation [T 2, ]. For OVO-Bench, we evaluate all backward, real-time, and forward splits. Backward and real-time questions are scored by accuracy. For the forward split, repetitive-event counting is scored by exact count matching, while sequential-step recognition and contextual-readiness recognition are scored using exact accuracy. We follow the benchmarks macro-averaging protocol across tasks for each split, and we further present the macro-averaging number over 3 splits. For StreamingBench, we evaluate the Real, Omni, Sequential-QA, and Proactive subsets base on how the benchmark annotations are organized. Real, Omni, and Sequential-QA are scored by accuracy. Following the original protocol, Sequential-QA includes the gold questionanswer history from earlier timestamps in the same video. For Proactive evaluation, the model is queried once per second until four seconds after the annotated trigger time. An example is counted as correct only when the model triggers within this tolerance 27 window, and its generated response contains the expected output. The overall StreamingBench score is the benchmark-weighted average over Real, Omni, Proactive, and Sequential-QA, using weights of 2,500, 1,500, 250, and 250 examples, respectively. C.4 Memory stress test In this section, we share additional implementation details for the memory stress test evaluation and the results presented in Table 3. We use the StreamArena (Zhang et al., 2026d) Historical Retrospection (HR) split as the benchmark, which has 877 questions across L1L4 over 237 videos. L1 to L4 indicate the evidence-to-query gap of less than 5 min, between 5 and 15 min, between 15 and 30 min, and longer than 30 min, respectively. We compare MaLoW (Qwen3.5-9B) against strong streaming video understanding models: MOSS-VLRealtime-11B (Wang et al., 2026), which retains the full historical context; VideoChat3-4B (Li et al., 2026) and AURA-8B (Lu et al., 2026), which operates with local 16 / 30 -second observation window, respectively; VST-7B (Guan et al., 2026), which compresses the historical observation as text-based memory. For AURA and VST, we follow the official implementations in StreamArena to evaluate the model performance. For MOSS-VL-Realtime, VideoChat3, and MaLoW, they share the same question prompt derived from the prompt used by AURA. MaLoW (Qwen3.5-9B) samples video frames at 1fps with maximum per-frame pixel budget of 262,144. The final two-second window is regarded as the current observation and will be sent to the VLMs, while the rest of the history frames will be sent to the MaLoW and converted into LoRA. The VideoChat3 uses 32 unique frames at 2 FPS from the latest 16 seconds, with an aspect-ratio-preserving maximum of 200,704 pixels per frame (4482). MOSS-VL samples frames at 1 FPS and with maximum per-frame pixel cap as 262,144 pixels. VST uses up to 384 causal-prefix frames at 1 FPS with aspect-ratiopreserving resolution determined dynamically by its 8,192-visual-token-per-segment budget. AURA takes most recent 30 seconds video at 1 FPS as input, with per-frame max pixel 602,112 pixel. C.5 Streaming Inference Speed Profiling We provide additional details on the inference-speed profiling reported in Figure 4. We measure the streaming inference latency of MaLoW and four baselines on 100 deterministically sampled OVO-Bench (Niu et al., 2025) questions spanning wide range of history lengths. Video durations range from 8 to 1,117 seconds, with median of 153.5 seconds, mean of 193.3 seconds, and 90th percentile of 312 seconds. This set includes both short clips and videos exceeding 10 minutes, enabling evaluation of long-context streaming efficiency. At each query timestamp t, we measure synchronized GPU computation required to process the current observation and answer the query under each methods native streaming protocol. Video decoding, resizing, and other input preprocessing are excluded. For MaLoW, each streaming step includes encoding the current observation, updating the hidden state and generating the LoRA adapter for the next time step, applying the adapter generated for the current time step, prefilling the model with the question and the two most recent frames from [t 2, t], and decoding the first output token. For SimpleStream (Qwen3.5-9B), the model receives only the question and two frames sampled from the most recent two-second window, [t 2, t], without earlier visual history. The measured latency includes prefilling with these inputs and decoding the first output token. For Qwen3.5-9B with full context, the measured latency includes prefilling the question together with the complete video history from the start of the stream to t, sampled at 1 FPS, followed by decoding the first output token. For VideoChat3, we follow its official streaming implementation. At each query, the model re-prefills the question together with sliding window of the most recent 32 frames, corresponding to approximately 16 seconds at 2 FPS, before generating the streaming response. sections.title: D Additional Experiments
sections.content: D.1 Ablation Study We conduct ablation studies with MaLoW (Qwen3.5-9B) to investigate key design choices: (1) the LoRA target modules, (2) the LoRA rank, (3) the architecture of the MaLoW, (4) the size of the current observation and (5) the refresh rate of the hidden state. All ablations are conducted on subset of an subset of the training data described in Section 3.4, rather than the final dataset used for the main experiments. Within each ablation, all training hyperparameters are kept fixed following Section 4.1, except for the component being ablated, ensuring controlled comparison. We report results on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench, together with the Episodic Memory (EPM) results from OVO-Bench. Where should LoRA be applied? Qwen3.5-9B adopts hybrid attention architecture in which one self-attention layer is interleaved with every four linear-attention layers, providing representative setting for studying LoRA placement in modern hybrid-attention VLMs. We evaluate three cumulative configurations: (1) applying LoRA only to the MLP layers shared by both self-attention and linear-attention blocks; (2) additionally applying LoRA to the v_proj in self-attention layers; and (3) further applying LoRA to the qkv_proj in linear-attention layers. As shown in Table 9, progressively extending LoRA to additional modules consistently improves the average performance, with the best results achieved when all three module types are adapted. What is the best LoRA rank? The results are presented in Table 10. Among the evaluated configurations, rank 8 achieves the best overall performance, with an average score of 69.2. Rank 4 performs slightly worse, suggesting limited adaptation capacity, whereas increasing the rank to 16 causes substantial performance drop on both benchmarks, indicating overfitting. What is the best MaLoW module structure? We investigate key design choices for the MaLoW module: (1) whether temporal modeling with State-Space Model (SSM) and global semantic aggregation are both necessary, and (2) how global semantics should be effectively preserved. Table 11 evaluates the contributions of the SSM and global semantic aggregation. The w/ sum variant achieves stronger performance on EPM, which emphasizes information from earlier observations, whereas the w/ SSM variant performs better on StreamingBench, where large portion of the evaluation focuses on real-time understanding. These results suggest that the SSM is particularly effective at modeling temporally local and causal information, while global semantic aggregation better preserves information over longer temporal horizons. Combining both components balances real-time understanding and long-term memory, yielding the best overall performance. Table 12 further compares different strategies for preserving global semantics. We consider three variants: sum, which directly accumulates all previous compact visual representations qt; weighted sum, which weights each qt according to the cosine similarity between adjacent temporal blocks; and gated sum, which selectively retains qt based on temporal similarity and is adopted in our final design. The gated sum achieves the best average performance. By filtering temporally redundant representations while retaining informative observations, the gating mechanism preserves global semantics more effectively and improves overall performance. How does the size of the current observation affect performance? Although the main experiments in Section 4.1 29 Table 11 Ablation study on the causal relationship and global semantics. To isolate the effect of the current observation window while keeping the hidden-state update interval fixed, we ablate the window sizes of 1, 2, and 4 seconds, with 2 seconds corresponding to our default setting. For the 4-second window, ht is updated using the oldest 2-second segment evicted from the window. For the 1-second window, MaLoW accumulates consecutive observations and updates ht after every 2 seconds of newly observed video. The result is presented in Table 13. larger 4-second current observation window improves real-time perception, as reflected by the higher StreamingBench score, but degrades memory performance, with EPM dropping to 60.0. In contrast, 1-second window reduces real-time perception while yielding similar EPM performance as the 2-second window. To balance real-time perception and long-term memory, we therefore use 2-second current observation window as the default setting. How does the refresh rate of the hidden state affect the performance? Although the main experiments in Section 4.1 treat each Ct as 2-second video clip, updating the hidden state ht every 2 seconds, the update frequency can be varied independently of the observation window. We therefore conduct an ablation with update intervals of 1, 2 (which used in the main experiments), and 4 seconds while keeping the base VLM input fixed to the most recent 2 seconds. For 1-second interval, the hidden state is updated using the oldest 1-second segment evicted from the current 2-second observation window; for 4-second interval, MaLoW accumulates newly observed video and updates the hidden state only after every 4 seconds of new observations. The results are presented in Table 14. We observe that less frequent updates, where each update incorporates larger temporal chunk, slightly improve memory performance at the cost of small drop in real-time perception. We hypothesize that this behavior is related to the State-Space Model (SSM) used for hidden-state updates. As shown in Table 11, the SSM primarily models short-term temporal dependencies. More frequent updates may therefore bias it toward shorter temporal ranges, improving current perception but slightly weakening longer-term memory, while less frequent updates have the opposite effect. Overall, performance remains stable across different update intervals. We therefore adopt 2-second interval, which balances memory and real-time perception while matching the current observation window for simpler design. D.2 Additional Analysis Latency Breakdown. We further analyze the latency of MaLoW (Qwen3.5-9B) reported in Figure 4, with the detailed breakdown presented in Table 15. Encoding the new frames and updating the hidden state ht, generating the LoRA tensors At+1 and Bt+1, and combining them to construct θt+1 account for 7.9%, 2.1%, and 3.7% of the total latency, respectively. Importantly, these operations compute the adapter for the next temporal block and can therefore be executed in parallel with applying θt and performing base-VLM prefilling and decoding for the current block. With such pipelining, only the application of θt and the wrapper overhead remain on the critical inference path, adding 1.75 ms to the 130.07 ms base-model inference latency. This corresponds to approximately 1.3% of the effective end-to-end latency, demonstrating that MaLoW introduces only marginal latency overhead in practical streaming inference. We compute V-JEPA-2 (Assran et al., 2025) surprise score on YouCook2 (Zhou et al., 2018) video by masking the features of the last temporal block and measuring the distance between its predicted representation and the representation of the subsequent block. We average the hidden states used to generate layer-specific LoRA adapters and project the resulting representation into two dimensions using t-SNE. We investigate whether long-term historical information compressed by MaLoW adversely affects real-time perception on the real-time splits of OVO-Bench and StreamingBench. For OVO-Bench, where video prefixes extend up to 28 minutes, we group real-time questions by their preceding video duration into four intervals: 05, 510, 1015, and over 15 minutes. As shown in Figure 8-1, MaLoW (Qwen3.5-9B) maintains comparable accuracy to the local-window baseline (Qwen3.5-9B, last 2 seconds) across different prefix ranges, suggesting that accumulated memory does not compromise real-time perception. For StreamingBench, where the original video prefixes are relatively short, we randomly sample 100 samples and construct longer streams by prepending randomly sampled videos, extending the historical context from 5 to 60 minutes. As shown in Figure 8-2, consistent with the observations on OVO-Bench, MaLoW (Qwen3.5-9B) maintains stable real-time perception across varying history lengths. These observations are consistent with our design choice to regularize the norm of the generated LoRA weights. This regularization constrains the magnitude of memory-induced weight updates, preventing them from dominating the pretrained model weights and disrupting its real-time perception capabilities.
